question.title: A/B Testing ML Models
question.scenario: An online retailer has two recommendation models: the current production model and a new model claiming 10% improvement. They need to validate the new model with real users before full deployment. The test should detect a 10% improvement with 95% confidence within 2 weeks. Business impact must be measured accurately.
question.question-text: Which approach provides statistically valid A/B testing for ML models?

choices.choice: Deploy new model to 50% of users immediately
Compare offline evaluation metrics from test datasets
Run both models on same requests and compare outputs
SageMaker endpoint with production variants and traffic splitting, with statistical significance monitoring

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider controlled experiments with random traffic assignment and proper statistical analysis.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: SageMaker production variants enable proper A/B testing. Configure endpoint with two variants - assign 90% traffic to production model (control) and 10% to new model (treatment). Random user assignment ensures unbiased comparison. Track business metrics (click-through rate, conversion, revenue) per variant. Calculate sample size for 10% effect detection with 95% confidence. Monitor until statistical significance reached. Offline metrics don't reflect real behavior. 50% immediately risks business impact. Shadow testing doesn't measure actual user response.

ul.li: Sample size calculation: n = 16 * variance / (effect_size^2) for 95% confidence
Variant weights control traffic percentage: VariantWeight parameter
CloudWatch metrics per variant enable comparison dashboards
Sequential testing methods allow early stopping when significance reached
Multi-armed bandit algorithms dynamically shift traffic to better performers

question.title: Data Validation Pipeline
question.scenario: A credit risk model retrains weekly on new application data. Last month, a data pipeline bug caused missing values in key features, leading to degraded model performance. The team needs automated data validation that catches quality issues before training, including schema validation, statistical checks, and anomaly detection.
question.question-text: Which approach implements comprehensive data validation?

choices.choice: SageMaker Processing job with data validation rules, integrated into training pipeline with conditional execution
Manual review of sample data before each training
Train model and evaluate performance to detect issues
Unit tests checking file existence only

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider automated validation integrated into ML pipelines with quality gates.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: SageMaker Processing with validation rules in the training pipeline provides systematic data quality checks. Define validation rules: schema checks (column types, names), statistical checks (null rates, distributions, value ranges), and anomaly detection (drift from baseline). Processing jobs execute these checks as a pipeline step. Conditional execution halts training if validation fails, preventing bad models. Results publish to CloudWatch for alerting. Manual review doesn't scale weekly. Training then detecting wastes resources. File existence doesn't validate content.

ul.li: Great Expectations library provides declarative data validation rules
SageMaker Pipelines ConditionStep branches based on validation results
Baseline statistics from training data establish expected distributions
Data profiling reports track quality metrics over time
Integration with Model Registry blocks registration of poorly-trained models

question.title: Model Security and Adversarial Robustness
question.scenario: A content moderation model classifies images as safe or unsafe. Adversaries attempt to bypass the model by adding imperceptible perturbations to unsafe images, causing misclassification. The team needs to detect adversarial inputs and improve model robustness against such attacks.
question.question-text: Which approaches improve model robustness against adversarial attacks?

choices.choice: Add CAPTCHA before classification
Encrypt the model weights
Use a larger model
Adversarial training with generated adversarial examples, input validation, and ensemble with diverse models

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider defense techniques that make models resilient to adversarial perturbations.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Defense-in-depth improves adversarial robustness. Adversarial training augments training data with adversarial examples (generated using FGSM, PGD attacks), teaching the model to correctly classify perturbed inputs. Input validation detects anomalous inputs - adversarial images often have unusual pixel distributions or high-frequency patterns. Ensembles of models with different architectures are harder to fool simultaneously - attacks optimized for one model often fail on others. Model encryption protects IP, not against adversarial inputs. Model size doesn't address adversarial robustness. CAPTCHA verifies humans, not content.

ul.li: FGSM (Fast Gradient Sign Method): single-step attack using gradient direction
PGD (Projected Gradient Descent): iterative attack, stronger than FGSM
Input preprocessing: JPEG compression, spatial smoothing remove perturbations
Certified defenses provide provable robustness within perturbation bounds
Adversarial detection: train classifier to distinguish clean vs adversarial inputs

question.title: Model Fairness Evaluation
question.scenario: A hiring platform uses an ML model to screen resumes. Regulators require demonstrating the model doesn't discriminate based on protected attributes (gender, race, age). The company needs to measure fairness metrics, identify potential bias, and document compliance. Some protected attributes aren't explicit features but may be correlated with other features.
question.question-text: Which approach provides comprehensive fairness evaluation?

choices.choice: Check if protected attributes are used as features
Manual review of rejected candidates
Compare average predictions across groups
SageMaker Clarify for pre-training data bias, post-training model bias, and SHAP-based feature attribution across groups

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Removing protected attributes from features isn't enough. Why might bias still creep in through correlated features?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: SageMaker Clarify provides multi-faceted fairness evaluation. Pre-training bias analysis detects imbalances in training data (class imbalance across groups). Post-training model bias measures outcome disparities using multiple metrics (demographic parity, equalized odds, disparate impact). SHAP analysis shows which features drive predictions differently across groups, catching proxy discrimination (e.g., zip code correlating with race). Clarify generates compliance-ready reports documenting bias assessment. Checking explicit features misses proxy discrimination. Simple average comparison misses nuanced disparities. Manual review doesn't scale and lacks metrics.

ul.li: Demographic parity: P(Y=1|A=0) ≈ P(Y=1|A=1) for protected attribute A
Equalized odds: equal TPR and FPR across groups
Disparate impact ratio: should be > 0.8 (four-fifths rule)
Proxy features: Clarify identifies features correlated with protected attributes
Model cards document fairness evaluation for regulatory compliance

question.title: Multi-Region ML Deployment
question.scenario: A global streaming service needs to deploy recommendation models across 5 AWS regions to serve users with low latency. Models should be consistent across regions. When models update, all regions should receive the new version within 1 hour. Regional failures shouldn't affect other regions. Model artifacts are 5 GB each.
question.question-text: Which architecture enables resilient multi-region ML deployment?

choices.choice: CloudFront caching inference responses
Single region serving all global traffic
Manual model copying to each region
S3 Cross-Region Replication for model artifacts, CodePipeline with parallel regional deployments, and Route 53 latency-based routing

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: How do you keep 5 GB model artifacts in sync across 5 regions within an hour without manual steps?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Multi-region architecture provides global low-latency with resilience. S3 Cross-Region Replication automatically copies model artifacts to regional buckets within minutes. CodePipeline deploys to all 5 regions in parallel when models update, achieving 1-hour rollout. Each region has independent SageMaker endpoints - regional failures are isolated. Route 53 latency-based routing directs users to nearest healthy region. Health checks fail over traffic if a region has issues. Single region adds latency for distant users. Manual copying doesn't meet 1-hour requirement. CloudFront can't cache dynamic recommendations.

ul.li: S3 replication time control (RTC) guarantees 15-minute replication SLA
CodePipeline cross-region actions deploy to multiple regions from single pipeline
Route 53 health checks detect endpoint failures for automatic failover
Global Accelerator provides static IPs with automatic regional failover
Endpoint naming convention includes region for deployment automation

question.title: Multimodal Data Fusion
question.scenario: A real estate valuation model needs to predict property prices using structured data (square footage, bedrooms, location), property images (interior, exterior), and text descriptions (agent listing descriptions). Each modality provides different information. The team needs to effectively combine these diverse data types into a unified model.
question.question-text: Which architecture fuses multimodal data for unified predictions?

choices.choice: Use only the most predictive single modality
Convert all data to tabular format
Separate encoders for each modality (tabular, CNN for images, transformer for text) with late fusion concatenating embeddings before final prediction layers
Average predictions from three separate models

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Images, text, and tabular data each need different processing. At what stage should their signals merge?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Late fusion with modality-specific encoders effectively combines multimodal data. Each encoder is optimized for its data type: tabular network for structured features, CNN (ResNet) for images extracting visual features (quality, style, views), transformer for text understanding listing language. Encoders produce fixed-size embeddings capturing modality-specific information. Concatenated embeddings feed into final prediction layers learning cross-modal interactions. This leverages each modality's strengths. Converting images/text to tabular loses rich information. Single modality ignores valuable signals. Separate model averaging misses cross-modal relationships.

ul.li: Early fusion: concatenate raw features before any processing
Late fusion: combine high-level representations from separate encoders
Cross-attention fusion: modalities attend to each other for richer interaction
Pretrained encoders: use frozen ImageNet CNN, BERT for text
Modality dropout: randomly drop modalities during training for robustness

question.title: Experiment Tracking and Reproducibility
question.scenario: A data science team of 10 people runs hundreds of experiments weekly testing different features, algorithms, and hyperparameters. They struggle to track which configurations produced the best results, reproduce successful experiments, and compare results across team members. Notebooks with embedded results are scattered across laptops.
question.question-text: Which approach provides systematic experiment management?

choices.choice: SageMaker Experiments with automatic metric logging, artifact tracking, and visual comparison tools
Spreadsheet logging experiment results manually
Git commits for each experiment
Email results to team members

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When 10 people run hundreds of experiments weekly, how do you avoid losing track of what worked and why?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: SageMaker Experiments provides centralized experiment management. Experiments organizes related runs into logical groups. Automatic tracking captures hyperparameters, metrics, and artifacts (model files, plots) without manual logging. Trial comparison visualizes metrics across experiments for selecting best configurations. Artifact storage enables reproducing any experiment by accessing exact inputs and outputs. Team members access shared experiment history. Lineage connects experiments to deployed models. Spreadsheets require manual entry and lack artifact tracking. Git commits don't capture metrics and results well. Email doesn't enable systematic comparison.

ul.li: Trial components: atomic units capturing inputs, outputs, parameters, metrics
Experiment analytics: query and filter experiments by parameter ranges
Automatic tracking in training jobs: metrics logged to Experiments automatically
Artifact versioning: track exact data and model versions for each trial
Integration with MLflow for teams already using MLflow tracking
